nameStory: The blue-foot gets its memorable common name from its distinctive blue coloring that appears at the base of its stem. When you handle this mushroom or it gets bruised, those blue tones become even more pronounced, making it look like it's wearing tiny blue socks!
description: Blue-foot is a small, slender mushroom that's quite rare to encounter in New England woodlands. It has a brownish cap that sits atop a thin stem with characteristic blue coloring at the base. This mushroom belongs to a group known for containing psychoactive compounds, so it's definitely a look-but-don't-touch species for foragers. Despite being uncommon, it's been documented 79 times in our region, so sharp-eyed nature lovers do occasionally spot them.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: The base of the stem shows distinctive blue coloring that intensifies when bruised or handled - this is the mushroom's signature feature

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Small brownish cap that may have subtle color variations, typically conical to bell-shaped when young

idTips.label: Bruising
idTips.description: Areas that are damaged or pressed will develop blue discoloration, especially noticeable on the stem

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Overall delicate and slender appearance - this isn't a chunky or robust mushroom

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: May have a faint earthy or flour-like odor, though often not particularly distinctive

habitat: Blue-foot grows in wooded areas throughout New England, typically found on decaying wood or in rich, moist soil with plenty of organic matter. Look for them in deciduous and mixed forests where there's good leaf litter and fallen branches. They seem to prefer areas with consistent moisture and partial shade.

seasonality.spring: Not typically active during spring months - the mycelium is likely developing underground but no visible fruiting bodies appear.
seasonality.summer: May begin appearing in late summer if conditions are right, particularly after periods of warm, humid weather with adequate rainfall.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for finding blue-foot mushrooms, especially during the cooler, damper days of autumn when many woodland fungi are most active.
seasonality.winter: Unlikely to find any specimens during winter months as cold temperatures halt their growth and development.

funFact: Blue-foot mushrooms contain the same psychoactive compounds found in the famous 'magic mushrooms' that have been used in cutting-edge medical research for treating depression and PTSD - all packed into these tiny, humble-looking fungi hiding in New England's forests!
confusionNotes: The blue bruising reaction helps distinguish blue-foot from many other small brown mushrooms, but several of its Psilocybe relatives also show blue coloring when damaged. The key is looking at the specific location - blue-foot shows this reaction most prominently at the stem base, like it's dipped in blue paint.
contextualKnowledge: This mushroom belongs to the Psilocybe genus, which has gained significant attention in recent years due to medical research into psychedelic therapy. However, these mushrooms remain federally controlled substances, and foraging them is illegal in most areas. They're best appreciated as fascinating examples of nature's chemistry rather than as something to collect.
compareHints: Among its Psilocybe relatives in New England, blue-foot is distinguished by its preference for woody substrates and its specific blue-staining pattern at the stem base. Liberty caps tend to have more pointed, conical caps and grow in grassy areas, while other Psilocybe species may show blue bruising in different locations or have different habitat preferences. The 'blue socks' appearance of the stem base is really blue-foot's calling card.
